name: Oral probiotics (BLIS K12)

lead: Oral probiotics such as BLIS K12 lozenges are meant to seed the mouth with friendly bacteria that compete with harmful ones. Breath-focused users take them hoping to reduce odor-producing species and get fresher breath.

The K12 strain of Streptococcus salivarius produces bacteriocin-like substances that can inhibit other bacteria, including strep throat bacteria. Lozenges are sold to support defence against more virulent streptococci. Breath-specific human evidence consists of a few small or registered trials, with no large published confirmation.

paras: They are dissolving lozenges, commonly taken after brushing so the strain can settle in the mouth, and often used after an antiseptic rinse. People generally use them over a stretch of days to weeks.
S. salivarius is usually harmless but is a rare opportunistic pathogen in people with very low white blood cell counts.

angle.text: BLIS K12 lozenges are taken for fresher breath by shifting the mouth's bacterial balance toward friendly strains and away from odor producers. Human data specific to breath is limited to a few small trials.

lead: Oral probiotics such as BLIS K12 are lozenges or tablets containing live bacteria intended to settle in the mouth and throat. BLIS K12 contains Streptococcus salivarius strain K12, which produces bacteriocin-like inhibitory substances (BLIS) that can hold back other bacteria.[1] People who use them for their looks are mostly after fresher breath: the idea is that a friendly bacterial population on the tongue and throat crowds out species that produce smelly sulfur compounds, which makes close conversation and smiling more comfortable.

S. salivarius is one of the first bacteria to colonize the mouth and upper airway, within hours of birth, and lozenges containing it are marketed to support defence against more virulent streptococci.[1] The K12 strain was characterised by a New Zealand research group led by John Tagg and colleagues, whose 2006 preliminary study in 23 people with halitosis is among the most cited K12 papers.[2] Later randomized trials and a 2025 systematic review of probiotics for halitosis have reported reductions in volatile sulfur compounds, with the largest and most lasting effects when probiotics are combined with tongue brushing.[2]

paras: S. salivarius is an early colonizer of the mouth and upper airway and is usually harmless, though it is an opportunistic pathogen that rarely enters the bloodstream in people with neutropenia.[1] BLIS-producing strains can inhibit other bacteria, including Streptococcus pyogenes, the cause of strep throat.[1]

K12 was developed first for throat health. Its genome carries a large plasmid encoding two lantibiotic bacteriocins, salivaricin A2 and salivaricin B, a feature reported by Hyink and colleagues in 2007 as the first single streptococcal strain known to make two distinct lantibiotics.[2] Breath freshness became a second common use because bacteria on the back of the tongue are the main source of volatile sulfur compounds. Products are sold as dissolving lozenges and tablets, commonly taken after brushing and tongue cleaning.

For appearance, K12 sits alongside tongue scraping, flossing and mouthwash in breath routines. Proponents describe it as a way to maintain a favorable bacterial population after cleaning, rather than only removing bacteria. Reviewers of halitosis note that most cases originate inside the mouth, which is why oral-microbe approaches are discussed.[2]

Users commonly describe taking a lozenge after the evening clean so that it dissolves undisturbed overnight, and pairing it with a tongue brush. Results in trials are described over days to weeks, and several reports note that benefits fade after the probiotic is stopped.[2][2]

In the 2006 preliminary study of 23 people with halitosis, participants rinsed with chlorhexidine and then used K12 or placebo lozenges. After one week, 85 percent of the K12 group and 30 percent of the placebo group showed reductions in volatile sulfur compounds above 100 ppb, and saliva bacterial profiles shifted in most K12 users.[2] A companion safety assessment examined antibiotic susceptibility, metabolic profile and virulence determinants of the strain.[2]

A 2025 systematic review of six randomized trials (360 participants) found probiotics often reduced volatile sulfur compounds and improved examiner-rated odor scores, particularly with S. salivarius K12 and Weissella cibaria, while noting heterogeneity between trials and limited long-term follow-up.[2] A 2026 randomized trial of 80 participants reported that probiotics, tongue brushing and the two combined each lowered sulfur compounds, with the combination producing the greatest reduction that largely persisted four weeks after the intervention ended.[2] A 2026 four-week trial of 117 adults compared K12 lozenges, a zinc mouthrinse and standard counseling; the zinc rinse gave the largest reduction in sulfur compounds, followed by the lozenges and then counseling alone.[2] A protocol published in 2025 plans to compare photodynamic therapy and K12 lozenges against standard hygiene in 92 adults with halitosis.[2]

A registered randomized trial of 120 orthodontic patients examined oral probiotics for hygiene and halitosis and is listed as completed.[3] A registered trial in nursery-age children examined K12 for preventing upper respiratory tract infection, a trial in 80 children has examined probiotics and oral health,[4] and a randomized trial published in 2021 examined the systemic immune response to ingesting BLIS K12.[5] Laboratory work from 2008 found that K12 lowered inflammatory signalling in cultured human airway cells.[2]

S. salivarius is generally a harmless member of the mouth flora, but it is a rare opportunistic pathogen that can enter the bloodstream in people with very low neutrophil counts.[1] Reviews of other probiotic genera note that bloodstream infections are uncommon but carry higher risk in people with severe underlying disease.[6] A 2025 trial of a genetically modified K12-derived strain in 29 healthy adults reported it was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events; it was not a halitosis study.[2]

K12 is used alongside tongue scraping, zinc-containing mouthrinses, flossing and chlorhexidine rinses. Other oral probiotic strains, such as Weissella cibaria and Lactobacillus salivarius products, are also studied for breath and gum health.[2]

lore.intro: On forums, K12 comes up in breath and oral-health routines as an add-on to tongue cleaning, sometimes alongside zinc rinses.[2]

claims.claim: K12 lozenges give fresher breath by changing the tongue bacteria
Probiotics work best with tongue brushing

timeline.event: Andrewes and Horder first describe Streptococcus salivarius.[1]
Burton and colleagues publish a preliminary study of K12 lozenges in 23 people with halitosis, and a safety assessment of the strain.[2]
Hyink and colleagues report that K12 carries a megaplasmid encoding salivaricins A2 and B.[2]
Cosseau and colleagues report K12 lowers inflammatory responses in cultured human epithelial cells.[2]
A review proposes S. salivarius as a model oral probiotic.[1]
A randomized trial on the systemic immune response to ingesting BLIS K12 is published.[5]
A systematic review of six randomized trials of probiotics for halitosis is published.[2]
Randomized trials compare probiotics with tongue brushing and zinc rinses for halitosis.[2]
